content.text:
# Hartwell Supply Co.: what you're looking at

Hartwell is a family-held HVAC/R distributor: about 150 people, twelve branches (Columbus, Cleveland, Cincinnati, Dayton, Toledo, Akron, Indianapolis, Fort Wayne, Louisville, Lexington, Troy MI and Pittsburgh), selling equipment, parts, refrigerant and supplies to heating and cooling contractors. The records run from 2016 to 2025.

**Its systems, each a separate database copied into the warehouse:**
- **ERP** (`erp_*`): customers and their account managers, the sales reps, products and vendors, sales orders and their lines (how each order arrived and who keyed it), purchase orders, transfers between branches, and returns.
- **Warehouse management** (`wms_*`): every stock movement (opening balances, receipts, sales, transfers, returns) and goods receipts. Stock on hand isn't stored anywhere: it's the running total of the movements.
- **Accounting** (`finance_*`): invoices and their lines, credit memos, customer payments, vendor bills and their lines, and vendor payments.
- **CRM** (`crm_*`): calls and emails to customer service, as logged by whoever took them; and the reps' quotes, with each quote's lines, its outcome (won, lost or expired), a loss reason when the rep entered one, and the order a won quote became.
- **External** (`external_*`): real monthly heating and cooling degree days and residential building permits for each branch's county.

**Days.** `day` is an operating day, about 21 a month; `dim_date` gives the calendar date.

**What isn't here:** profitability by customer, rep or branch; why a return happened; whether an order was keyed correctly; whether a vendor bill was right. Like any real business, those have to be worked out from the records, and some of them can't be.

WITH pc AS (SELECT invoice_id, count(*) np, sum(amount) pamt, min(day) pday FROM finance_customer_payments GROUP BY 1)
SELECT d.year, count(*) inv, sum(CASE WHEN pc.invoice_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) unpaid, sum(CASE WHEN pc.invoice_id IS NULL THEN i.amount ELSE 0 END) unpaid_amt,
 sum(CASE WHEN np>1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) multi_pay, sum(CASE WHEN pc.invoice_id IS NOT NULL AND abs(pamt-i.amount)>0.01 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) amt_mismatch,
 sum(CASE WHEN pc.invoice_id IS NOT NULL THEN i.amount-pamt ELSE 0 END) short_paid, min(i.day) minday, max(i.day) maxday
FROM finance_invoices i JOIN dim_date d ON d.day=i.day LEFT JOIN pc USING(invoice_id) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

content.text:
My verdict on F7 is **stands with changes**. I saved the challenge as `challenge.json`.

**What held up:**
- **The groups predict ahead.** I sorted customers into the three groups using only 2016-19 data. The 152 classed very slow went on to pay 31.17 days late in 2020-24 and held 29.0% of the overdue balance on 5.3% of billing (q331).
- **No outside factor explains the groups.** I checked customer size, invoice size, tenure, discount, credit memos, "Invoice question" contacts and month of the year, and the groups barely differ on any of them (q336, q339). How many very slow accounts each rep has varies only a little more than chance would give (q337).
- **The sizing reproduces.** Re-running it gives the same 2,980,324 average overdue balance and 136,567.16 a year (q343).

**What changed:**
1. **"A stable trait of each customer" is too strong.** Within each group, a customer's lateness has almost no year-to-year correlation: 0.021, 0.013 and -0.061 (q341). The 0.94 correlation comes from the gaps between the three groups. Which group a customer is in persists; their position inside it doesn't, so there's no meaningful "worst" among the 326.
2. **A list made in advance catches about 29% of overdue dollars, not 33%.** Another 18.5% of later overdue dollars came from customers who couldn't have been classed beforehand (q331).
3. **The 2025 low point (30.3%) is not an improvement.** The cited queries drop unpaid invoices, and all 21,848 unpaid invoices are from 2025. 28.5% of very slow customers' 2025 invoices are unpaid, against 15.7% for prompt payers (q322, q327). The 2016-24 sizing isn't affected.
4. **"Limits are no more generous" says little.** Credit limits don't track customer billing at all (correlation -0.009, q347), so equal limits across groups don't test credit policy.
5. **The 136,567 a year is the top of a range.** It assumes both slow groups come down to prompt lateness, an 8% cost of capital and no lost sales. A more cautious case (very slow brought only to the slow group's level, at 5%) is 36,088 a year. The 0.72M–1.71M of receivables freed is a one-time cash release; only the carrying cost recurs (q343).

The recommendation stays the same: a credit/AR review of the very slow group, then the slow group, rather than tightening everyone's terms. I'd add a control group to the pilot. The groups are so regular, with no within-group persistence and no seasonality, that they may reflect how the records were produced rather than how customers actually pay.
